title: Heatmap from Points: See Where Points Cluster
description: Turn coordinate rows into a density heatmap with the Heatmap from Points tool — clusters and hot spots visualised locally in the browser. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, 5,000 delivery stops plotted as a heatmap reveal the two neighbourhoods that generate half the work — structure invisible in the spreadsheet and obvious in the glow.
quick_answer: The Heatmap from Points tool loads coordinate rows and visualises where they cluster, as a simple density view in your browser. Paste or drop the points and read the pattern — hot spots, cold gaps and the shape of the data — before any formal statistics begin.
steps_intro: A thousand rows of lat/lon hide their story. Heat shows it:

body.t: Stops, calls and orders as points glow where the work concentrates — depot and territory decisions start from this picture. Sparse data cleans up first with the
Reports, sightings and incidents cluster for reasons — the heatmap is the first look that suggests where to ask why.
Sightings density hints at habitat use — a hypothesis generator, honestly labelled as such, before effort-corrected analysis.
A suspicious hot spot at a round coordinate (or at 0,0) is the classic data-entry artefact — heatmaps catch what row counts never will.

A sales dataset glows brightest at head office — because un-geocoded rows defaulted to the HQ address. The heatmap did not show demand; it showed a data pipeline. Both readings are valuable; only one is true.

A small radius draws many tight hot spots (individual venues); a large radius merges them into districts. Neither is 'correct' — the radius is an editorial choice, and the honest analyst reports which one the picture used.

popular_table.note: This is a density visualisation, not a kernel-density statistical surface with bandwidth inference. It shows where points are; conclusions about why remain yours.

faq: Is this a true kernel density estimate?

It is a simple density view — points contribute glow around themselves and the picture aggregates them. Formal KDE with bandwidth selection and edge correction is GIS-statistics work; this page is the honest first look, labelled as such.
Coordinate rows — CSV-style lat/lon lists and pasted pairs. Messy files clean up in the CSV coordinate tools first; the heatmap wants two numeric columns it can trust.
No — density is order-blind. Duplicates matter: identical rows stack glow, which the deduplicator exists to tame.
A plain density view counts each point once. Weighted analysis (by sales, severity, population) belongs to fuller GIS tooling.
The map looks different at each zoom.
Density rendering responds to scale — features merge as you zoom out. Fix the zoom when comparing two datasets' pictures, or the comparison is theatre.
They mean no points. Absence of records and absence of activity are different facts — the map shows the first; only you know the second.
Aggregate glow is actually a privacy-friendlier way to share patterns than pins, but dense rural points can still identify. Round coordinates before sharing if the data is personal.
